title: The fundamental theorem of algebra: the complex numbers are algebraically closed

standard_prerequisites: The intermediate value theorem from calculus: every odd degree real polynomial has a real root, by sign change of the dominating leading term
Galois theory for finite extensions: for a finite Galois extension with group G and a subgroup P, the fixed field K^P has degree over the base equal to the index of P in G
The 2-sylow theorem: every finite group has a 2-sylow subgroup, and the index of a 2-sylow subgroup is odd
Up to isomorphism the only degree two extension of the reals is the complex numbers, and every complex number has a square root, so the complex numbers admit no quadratic extension
Fields, Lemma lemma-normal-closure: every finite extension can be embedded in a finite normal extension over the base
core_obligations: Every odd degree real polynomial has a real root: for large positive and large negative inputs the dominating odd-degree term changes sign, so the intermediate value theorem gives a zero; hence the reals admit no nontrivial odd degree field extension

Let K over the reals be finite Galois with group G and let P be a 2-sylow subgroup; the fixed field K^P over the reals has odd degree the index of P, hence equals the reals, which forces P equal to G; so G is a 2-group

If G is nontrivial then the complex numbers sit inside K, since the complex numbers are up to isomorphism the only degree two extension of the reals; if G had more than two elements, K over the complex numbers would give a quadratic extension of the complex numbers, which is absurd because every complex number has a square root; hence K equals the complex numbers

Finally, if the complex numbers were not algebraically closed there would be a nontrivial finite extension K over the complex numbers, which embeds in its normal closure over the reals by the normal closure lemma, giving a finite Galois extension of the reals that must equal the complex numbers; contradiction; hence the complex numbers are algebraically closed
proof_roadmap: Record the calculus input on odd degree real polynomials
Force the Galois group of any finite Galois extension of the reals to be a 2-group of order at most two
Conclude via the normal closure that no nontrivial finite extension of the complex numbers exists
